newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges passage of higher cigarette tax.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges passage of higher cigarette tax.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday strongly urged Congress to hike cigarette taxes by 20 cents a pack and use the money to provide health care for up to half of America's 10 million uninsured children.

At a White House ceremony held to celebrate a childhood immunisation milestone -- more than 90 percent of U.S. 2-year-olds are now being vaccinated against preventable diseases -- Clinton also announced that he and his wife Hillary will hold a day-long conference on the strengths and weaknesses of the nation's child care system on Oct. 24.

"This 20-cent increase in the cigarette tax not only will provide necessary resources to protect and improve children's health. By raising the price of cigarettes, it will discourage children from starting to smoke in the first place. It is the right thing to do," Democrat Clinton said.

The proposed increase in cigarette taxes has passed the Senate, but not the House of Representatives. Clinton said it would add another $8 billion to the $16 billion already included in his balanced budget agreement with Republican congressional leaders to expand child health care.
"It has literally been a generation since we did anything this much for children's health insurance. We mustn't waste it," he said.
The 90 percent immunisation achievement realised a goal set by President Jimmy Carter, the last Democrat to occupy the White House.

"Now record numbers of our children, our youngest and most vulnerable children, are actually safe from potentially deadly diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, measles, polio and meningitis," Clinton said.
Even with the high level of immunisation, almost 1 million American children under age 2 still lack one or more of their recommended vaccinations.
To try to close the gap, Clinton ordered Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala to start working with states on an integrated immunisation registry system.
"That's the kind of thing most people can't remember, but it may have something to do with whether their children live or die," he said.
He also said all children who attend federally subsidised child-care centres would be required to be immunised.

"Since so many of our youngest children spend at least part of their days in child care outside the home, this, too, can be an important step in our efforts to reach some of the children still falling through the cracks," Clinton said.
